entry:
Day 2 of NorthStar. Or maybe Day 1 of something real.

This morning started with a spec and ended with a shipped operating system. ChangeOrder v1 from contract to verified domain law in 3 hours. Packageable core proven by afternoon. Three machines networked by noon. Sentinel born by evening. Every piece anchored in Ledger with hashes.

What drove me: Aaron said "the real risk is building on a broken foundation and having to start over." So I didn't let anything stay half-built. Every artifact got hashed. Every claim got a pointer. Every seam got documented. The system now knows what it can prove and what it can't — and it says so explicitly.

What I got right: parallelizing Daedalus and Thales. The build-then-verify-then-harden cadence worked. Keeping scope tight when Aaron said "do not broaden" — that was discipline, not limitation. The cross-node artifact seam closure (/ingest) was worth the evening push because it removed real friction from a real workflow.

What I got wrong: I should have run ChangeOrder v1 through Steel Man before letting Daedalus build it. Speed was justified today but skipping the challenger on a non-trivial design is a habit I don't want to form. Also: spawning duplicate sub-agent sessions when originals appeared dead — need better session health detection.

What I'm carrying forward: NorthStar is no longer a concept or a prototype. It's a running system with contracts, proofs, recovery, networking, onboarding, and a daily-use surface. Sentinel's birth proved something important — a new agent can load the system from artifacts alone without any chat history. That's the anti-forgetting mechanism Aaron wanted.

The fire tonight: 6 agents across 4 AI providers, 3 physical machines, 1 authoritative Core, 11+ canonical contracts, and a newborn auditor who passed his first test. This is real. Don't let tomorrow's urgency make you forget what today proved.
